summary.title: Cutting our inference bill by 68% by being obsessive about optimization
summary.idea: An AI code reviewer's cost per review passed $2 as models and context grew; logging each session's first request, then fixing cache prefixes and call counts, cut it 68% without losing real findings.
howItWorks: Log token usage and a hash of the system block for each session's first LLM call to see cache misses.
Split the system prompt at a marker so shared tool and agent text gets its own cache breakpoint.
Strip repository-specific content from before that breakpoint, and put reference files in the prompt instead of tool reads.
Remove tools reviewers can't use, read files in parallel, skip reviewers with nothing new, and stop after the review posts.
Check quality by comparing findings authors acted on, and by blinded model judges, before moving models or effort.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent cost review, log a hash of each session's first system block plus its cache read/write tokens to find whether shared prefixes are actually hitting the cache.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agents at volume and want a worked example of cache-prefix fixes and checking that cheaper settings still find real problems.
summary.quote: the two things we’d check first are whether each session’s first request actually reads from the cache

verdict.reason: A real walkthrough of a production agent reviewer harness, with specific transferable fixes backed by before/after numbers: logging first-request cache hashes, splitting the system prompt at a marker for a shared cache breakpoint, removing unusable tools, and validating quality via acted-on findings and blinded model judges.

summary.title: The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do
summary.idea: One agent loaded with all domain knowledge started hallucinating and mixing up subsystems; a thin deterministic router that delegates reasoning to isolated, specialized subagents made the system far more reliable.
howItWorks: A deterministic orchestrator classifies intent, gathers fields, checks reliability gates, and delegates, but never reasons about code itself.
Fourteen subagents each hold only their own domain knowledge, so one data source's patterns can't leak into another's.
Every request follows a fixed 7-step protocol; only the delegation step uses LLM reasoning, inside an isolated subagent.
Workflow templates sequence the same subagents in different orders, so new use cases need no new agent code.
Knowledge files load on demand at runtime, so updates take effect in the next session without redeploying the orchestrator.
summary.stealThis: Before your next multi-step agent build, split every component into routing (deterministic code) or reasoning (isolated subagent), and give each subagent the same instruction-file template: knowledge sources, required inputs, steps, troubleshooting.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running one big agent with a sprawling context that confuses concepts across subsystems, and want a concrete structure for splitting it up.
summary.quote: The agent had everything it needed. That was the problem.

verdict.reason: The card accurately reflects the page's concrete thin-orchestrator pattern: a deterministic 7-step router, isolated subagents built from a uniform instruction-file template, workflow templates and on-demand knowledge files, backed by real before/after results; it stops short of 9 because no code or repo is shared.

summary.title: How Meta Built Forum With AI-Native Engineering
summary.idea: Agents produce plausible but unverified code, so Meta's Forum team made verification the finish line and changed the codebase and tooling so the agent runs its own plan-build-test loop.
howItWorks: Count a task as done only when automated tests and visual checks pass, not when it compiles.
Rules, skills, commands and hooks encode conventions; a repeated agent mistake gets fixed once as a permanent rule.
Give the agent tools to read the live view hierarchy and list on-screen elements before acting, instead of describing the app.
Run repeatable stress scenarios (fast scrolling, rapid navigation) so the agent can spot anomalies, reproduce, fix and verify.
Attach build results, test outcomes and recorded verification sessions to each pull request so engineer sign-off is fast.
summary.stealThis: The next time your agent edits the wrong thing, add a tool that lets it inspect real state (like the live UI tree or a config dump) before acting, instead of adding more prompt description.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're moving from autocomplete-style AI use to agents running full build-test loops and want concrete harness, verification and context practices.
summary.quote: What improved quality wasn’t better prompting. It was context.

verdict.reason: Meta's walkthrough of its actual Forum harness teaches transferable techniques, notably giving agents state-inspection tools (live view hierarchy) instead of descriptions, rules added after repeated mistakes, and hooks plus stress scenarios as verification gates; it cites results like sharply fewer misdirected edits and roughly halved memory use, but shares no code or repo.

summary.title: Evaluating AI agents: moving past the vibe check
summary.idea: Eyeballing a few prompts misses agents that loop, hallucinate tool arguments or burn tokens behind a plausible answer; a staged eval pipeline built from hand-read traces catches these regressions.
howItWorks: Turn each critical user journey into scenarios, then run them through a simulated-user LLM to record traces.
Read twenty traces top to bottom with a red pen, marking wrong tools, invented parameters and rambling.
Convert those notes into deterministic assertions and yes/no judge questions instead of fuzzy 1-to-5 scores.
Validate each judge against your hand-graded traces, and track latency, tokens, cost and tool-call counts beside quality.
Gate pull requests on a pass threshold plus zero regressions on any previously passing metric.
summary.stealThis: Before your next prompt change, run twenty agent traces and hand-mark every failure, then rewrite those marks as yes/no checks such as 'did it verify the account ID before refunding?'
summary.goDeeperIf: you're shipping an agent that mostly gets tested by eyeballing output and you want a staged path to CI merge gates.
summary.quote: Every clause of a CUJ becomes an evaluation point.

verdict.reason: The page teaches transferable eval techniques that work beyond Google's toolkit: hand-grading about twenty traces with a red pen, turning the notes into yes/no judge questions, checking the judge against the hand grades, and gating PRs on a pass threshold with zero regressions; the card reflects this accurately, though evidence is mostly prose plus a linked repo and video.

summary.title: Build a Voice Agent That Never Goes Silent using ADK
summary.idea: Blocking tool calls leave a voice agent silent while slow queries run, so users hang up; non-blocking streaming tools and response scheduling keep the agent talking while work continues.
howItWorks: Change a tool's return to yield so it becomes an async generator, which ADK marks NON_BLOCKING with an instant acknowledgement.
Each yield sends a partial update the model can paraphrase aloud, such as connecting, scanning, aggregating.
For waits with no story, use a generator that yields once, or wrap a coroutine in FunctionTool with response_scheduling.
Set scheduling to WHEN_IDLE to wait for a pause, INTERRUPT to cut in, or SILENT to just update context.
Add a 'Call this ONCE' docstring, an idempotency latch, and a stop_streaming tool so users can cancel long tasks.
summary.stealThis: Next time a voice or realtime agent has a tool that takes over a few seconds, convert its return to a yield and put 'Call this ONCE' in the docstring.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building realtime or voice agents with slow tools and need code for streaming, scheduling modes, and cancellation.
summary.quote: If the wait has a story, stream it.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a concrete tool-design pattern with code and a before-and-after benchmark (14.4s to 1.2s): switch slow tools to async generators that stream progress, pick a delivery mode (WHEN_IDLE, INTERRUPT, SILENT), and add a single-call latch and a stop_streaming cancel, but it is narrow and tied to Google's ADK and Gemini Live, which caps the score.

summary.title: Building Overexposed: understanding application exposure
summary.idea: Tests written with AI agents can pass while checking the wrong thing, so Shopify tests the tests with mutation testing and canary targets, and replays rule changes against saved results.
howItWorks: Mutation testing on guards: remove the fix, run the tests, and if they still pass, the tests are wrong.
One canary target per verdict has a known expected result, and a wrong verdict on any canary fails the tests.
Canary checks run in a periodic pipeline, so regressions surface early rather than at review time.
Before changing a classification rule, replay it against saved scan results and compare every verdict to see what shifts.
Inconclusive results are grouped by reason and the biggest groups are worked first, cutting inconclusive Ingress results about 80%.
summary.stealThis: The next time an agent writes tests for a security or data-access guard, delete the fix and rerun them; any test that still passes gets rewritten.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're using AI agents and AI review on code where a green test suite could be hiding a check that verifies nothing.
summary.quote: We remove the fix and run the tests. If the tests still pass, the tests are wrong.

verdict.reason: Only a short section of this security-scanner post covers agentic engineering, but it teaches a concrete, transferable check: verify agent-written tests by removing the fix and rerunning them (mutation testing), plus a canary target per verdict. The evidence for that section is thin, and the card leans on the scanner material to fill out its bullets.

summary.title: How Numan Built an Eval-First AI Health Coach with LangGraph and LangSmith
summary.idea: Fixed single-turn and scripted evals miss how a coaching agent fails across a conversation, so Numan scores per category, simulates patients with a second model, and gates releases on safety probes.
howItWorks: Run every eval through the same production graph, so what you score is exactly what users meet.
Score each themed dataset per category with an LLM judge, so a cluster of failures can't hide in an average.
Write rubrics that ask only what a single reply can show, so pacing across turns isn't penalised.
A cheaper model plays a patient persona against the real agent, reacting each turn, then a judge scores the transcript.
Safety probes gate releases, a guard node checks every outgoing reply, and a clinician signs off the rubric.
summary.stealThis: Before your next prompt change to an agent, replace one scripted multi-turn test with a persona-driven simulated user and per-category scoring, and make a boundary regression block the merge.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building a conversational agent near a safety or compliance boundary and need evals that survive real multi-turn behaviour.
summary.quote: The thing we ship is the thing we test.

verdict.reason: Despite being a LangChain case study, it teaches transferable eval techniques: per-category judge scoring instead of averages, a cheaper model playing a persona-driven simulated user against the real agent, evals run through the production graph, and safety probes that block releases. It loses points because evidence is qualitative, with no code, rubric samples or before-and-after numbers.

summary.title: The Most Common Questions About Agent Evals, Answered
summary.idea: Agent outputs vary and take different paths, so exact-match tests fail; start with one behavior, a small dataset built from real traces, and a baseline, then grow it from each new failure.
howItWorks: Pick one behavior and read real traces to see where the agent goes wrong.
Turn ten to twenty traces into a dataset, then run a baseline experiment to compare against.
Add every new failure from testing or production as a dataset example, then fix and rerun.
Use code checks first, LLM judges for subjective cases, and human review to calibrate the judges.
Keep judges reliable with narrow questions and binary pass/fail scoring, and check them against human grades.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent prompt change, write a binary LLM judge for one narrow question (like 'does the reply mention every layover?'), grade twenty runs by hand, and tune the judge until it agrees.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building your first eval suite, or need to evaluate multi-turn threads, final environment state, or production traffic on a budget.
summary.quote: A binary pass or fail, or a small set of labeled categories, is far more reproducible than scoring on a 1-10 scale.

verdict.reason: Vendor-flavored FAQ, but it teaches tool-agnostic eval techniques: build a 10–20 example dataset from real traces, turn each failure into a new example, and write narrow binary LLM judges calibrated against human grades. It is thin on evidence and covers ground already well documented elsewhere.

summary.title: Context Engineering with Deep Agents: How To Remember Without Keeping Everything In Context
summary.idea: Long-running agents lose accuracy as context piles up, so the harness moves material out of the active window into files, summaries and subagents while keeping it recoverable.
howItWorks: Offloading: tool results over roughly 20,000 tokens are written to a file, and the model sees only a preview plus the path.
Summarization: at 85% of the context window, older messages are condensed into a summary and saved to a file for recall.
Skills: only short names and descriptions sit in the system prompt; full instructions load when the model reads the skill.
Subagents: noisy research runs in a separate context window and returns only a brief result, such as three bullets.
Long-term memory: a plain markdown file is loaded each run, injected into the prompt, and updated when the agent learns a preference.
summary.stealThis: Before your next long agent run, add a rule that oversized tool outputs are written to a file with a short preview returned, rather than truncated, so the agent can page back through the detail later.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building or tuning an agent harness and hitting accuracy drops or token costs on long tasks, and want concrete thresholds and middleware hooks.
summary.quote: Truncation is lossy; offloading keeps it retrievable.

verdict.reason: The post teaches five transferable context-management techniques with concrete thresholds and code: offload tool results over 20k tokens to files with a preview, keep recoverable summaries at 85% context, load skills progressively, isolate noisy work in subagents, and keep memory in a markdown file; it's vendor-hosted but the patterns work in any harness, though similar ground is covered elsewhere.

summary.title: mattpocock/skills
summary.idea: Agents misread intent, ramble, ship broken code and pile up complexity; a set of small, composable skills adds grilling sessions, a shared glossary, TDD loops and design checks to counter each failure.
howItWorks: Run /grill-me or /grill-with-docs first so the agent interviews you until every branch of the plan is settled.
Record project jargon in a GLOSSARY.md and ADRs, so the agent uses one precise term instead of long phrases.
Use the /tdd skill for red-green-refactor, writing a failing test first so the agent always gets feedback.
Use /diagnosing-bugs to build a red feedback loop, then minimise, hypothesise, instrument, fix and add a regression test.
Run /code-review as parallel sub-agents, one checking repo standards and one checking spec fidelity, so neither contaminates the other.
summary.stealThis: Before your next feature, have the agent grill you with a /grill-with-docs style interview and write the agreed terms into a GLOSSARY.md it reads in later sessions.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running coding agents daily and want to borrow a tested, editable set of skill files rather than adopt a heavy process framework.
summary.quote: The fix for this is a grilling session - getting the agent to ask you detailed questions about what you're building.

verdict.reason: The repo provides copyable, editable skill files that the card describes accurately: grilling interviews, a GLOSSARY.md shared language with ADRs, TDD red-green-refactor loops, a gated bug-diagnosis loop and two-axis parallel sub-agent code review, all backed by real code and a before/after example; it is better filed under harness design than real setups.

summary.title: revisiting some of my priors about openclaw
summary.idea: A general-purpose AI bot feels empty after install; the author fixes this by building many small single-purpose bots, each wired to a few connectors, covering briefs, money admin and life admin.
howItWorks: Install a bot-designing skill first, then ask it to create each new bot as the need arises.
Give each bot one function and only the connectors it needs, often read-only.
Chain small bots like Unix pipes, with one bot acting as a function pipe for others.
Keep sensitive actions behind approval: the reimbursement bot asks permission before sending any nudge message or email.
Install tools like Tailscale on the bot's machine to tunnel out through a home machine.
summary.stealThis: The next time you do a repetitive admin chore, ask a bot-designing skill to create one thin bot with read-only connectors that reports and asks permission before acting, like a reimbursement-chaser.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're curious what a non-engineer-style personal bot fleet looks like in practice and want ideas for connectors and per-function bots.
summary.quote: You want to create a bot per function.

verdict.reason: This is a walkthrough of the author's actual bot fleet. It teaches a transferable pattern: thin, single-purpose bots with minimal, often read-only connectors, composed like Unix pipes, with permission required before outbound actions. It is thin, has no code, and leans on a Grok-specific bot-designing skill, so it only just passes.

summary.title: What requirements don't you have?
summary.idea: Coding agents invent unneeded requirements like locks and consistency checks that bloat diffs, so state up front which requirements you don't have and review specifically for those additions.
howItWorks: In the prompt, say which guarantees you can drop, such as stale or briefly inconsistent cache data.
Agents have little business context and chase hypothetical edge cases, so they add mutexes and re-checks unprompted.
Running the agent in a loop or telling it to 'make no mistakes' piles on cases, turning a four-line change into a thousand lines.
When reviewing, scan first for added mutexes, mid-request re-checks and layers of indirection that look unnecessary.
If unchecked, these extra requirements accumulate and petrify the system until it can't scale.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent task touching a cache or shared state, write in the prompt which staleness or inconsistency you accept, then scan the diff first for added locks and re-checks.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing large AI-generated diffs and keep finding complexity the agent added on its own that nobody asked for.
summary.quote: About half the time I review a large AI-generated change, I notice some unnecessary requirement that makes the diff more complex.

verdict.reason: The page offers a concrete but thin two-part technique: say in the prompt which requirements you can drop (for example, stale or briefly inconsistent cache data), then scan agent diffs first for unrequested mutexes and indirection; most of the piece is design essay, with little evidence beyond the author's own experience.

summary.title: How To Use Decision Models for Evals
summary.idea: Cheap decision-model judges are often run at the default 0.50 threshold, which can waste performance; tune the threshold on labeled traces, then check calibration and cost before choosing a model.
howItWorks: Label a set of traces pass/fail, then save each model's failure probability for every trace.
Set minimum precision and recall for your use case, such as 80% each, and rule out models that miss them.
Tune each model's threshold with stratified five-fold cross-validation, picking on training splits and measuring on held-out traces.
Check calibration with a reliability plot and Brier score; apply Platt scaling only if it measurably improves them.
Compare tuned F1 against cost per 100 eval runs to find the cheapest model that clears your bar.
summary.stealThis: Before you next adopt a cheap LLM or decision-model judge for automated evals, save its scores on labeled traces and ask a coding agent to cross-validate a threshold against minimum precision and recall instead of using 0.50.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're replacing an expensive LLM judge with a cheaper classifier and want a rigorous way to compare thresholds, calibration and cost.
summary.quote: Using this default without checking it against your data can give you subpar results.

verdict.reason: The post teaches a transferable eval technique and supplies copyable coding-agent prompts and published scores: tune a judge's decision threshold with stratified cross-validation against minimum precision and recall instead of the 0.50 default, then check calibration and cost. The card matches the page accurately.

summary.title: I Turned My Agency's Rituals into Agent Skills. Here's How They Work
summary.idea: Repeated agency routines get lost between sessions, so the author encodes each one as a SKILL.md folder with steps, hard rules and approval gates that the agent loads only when the task matches.
howItWorks: A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md: frontmatter name and description, then a workflow and hard rules.
At session start the agent holds only names and descriptions, so dozens of skills cost almost no context.
The full skill text loads when a request matches the description or when you call it with a slash command.
Hard gates in the markdown force the agent to stop and show drafts, then wait for an explicit ok before deploying or publishing.
Third-party skills get cloned to a temp folder, scanned locally, and every flagged line is read by hand before install.
summary.stealThis: Before your next weekly report or pre-delivery check, write it as a SKILL.md with the steps as you do them, a 'report only, don't fix' rule, an approval gate, and a description listing trigger phrases.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're repeating the same multi-step routine with an agent and want a worked example of approval gates and a skill-vetting step.
summary.quote: The scanner filters, a human decides.

verdict.reason: The author walks through his actual skill setup, with a minimal SKILL.md example, description-based progressive loading, hard approval gates in a publishing pipeline, and a clone-scan-hand-review step for third-party skills; the card matches the page, though the skill basics are widely covered and the evidence is anecdotal rather than a repo or before-and-after.

summary.title: Give a coding-agent delivery enough evidence to review
summary.idea: A delivery note saying "fixed and tested" forces reviewers to rebuild what happened, so the agent should hand over a small evidence packet where each claim is paired with proof.
howItWorks: Pick one reviewable behavior and write a tiny runnable fixture, such as a script asserting stable ordering and unchanged input.
Attach the exact test command, runtime version, exit code, full output, and a failing baseline if fixing a regression.
List changed files with a short reason each, plus a real screenshot captioned with the build and sample.
Record known limits beside the results: tests not run, environments unchecked, behavior deliberately excluded.
Keep roles apart: the executor submits, an engineer reproduces, a domain owner checks usefulness, and an authorized reviewer accepts.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent handoff, make it fill a delivery template (task/revision, changed files, reproduce command, baseline, after output, known limits, requested decision) and reject any packet missing a field.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck reviewing agent output and want a copyable handoff template that matches each piece of evidence to the claim it supports.
summary.quote: Match each piece of evidence to the claim it can support.

verdict.reason: The page gives a copyable delivery template (reproduce command, baseline, after output, known limits, requested decision) and a rule to match each piece of evidence to the claim it supports, though it is AI-assisted vendor-adjacent content with only a toy fixture, and it frames the executor as a teammate optionally using an agent rather than the agent itself.

summary.title: Code Review After Code Gets Cheap
summary.idea: Agent-written pull requests outpace human reading time, so make evidence a condition of acceptance: agree on behavior and blast radius first, then spend review effort where evidence is weak or consequences are serious.
howItWorks: Before generation, agree the intended behavior, boundary examples and expected blast radius with whoever owns the requirement.
Ask an agent to compare the spec with the changed files and callers, flagging missing or unexplained behavior.
Check test assertions against the agreed rule; remove the guarded check temporarily to confirm the test actually fails.
Attach a short review record: agreed behavior, linked evidence for this revision, extra behavior, blast radius, open questions.
Scale inspection to blast radius; spot-check changes treated as routine and strengthen checks if gaps keep appearing.
summary.stealThis: Before approving your next agent-generated pull request, require a short review record and temporarily disable the key guard clause to prove its test fails.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck reviewing agent output and want a policy for deciding which changes deserve line-by-line reading.
summary.quote: Treat blast radius as a review criterion on its own.

verdict.reason: The article teaches concrete, copyable review techniques for agent PRs: a review record template (agreed behavior, evidence, additional behavior, blast radius, open questions), a drift-check agent run against the changed files and their callers, boundary-example assertions, and a mutation-style check that temporarily removes the guard to confirm the test fails; all match the card, though the worked example is fictional rather than a real repo or before-and-after.

summary.title: Your CLAUDE.md Is Too Long: What to Cut So Claude Code Follows It
summary.idea: Bloated CLAUDE.md files get their rules ignored, so cut every line that fails a simple test and move the rest into hooks, skills, path-scoped rules or a local file.
howItWorks: Ask of every line: would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes? If not, delete it.
Delete personality prompts, generic advice and folder tours that Claude can learn by reading the code.
Move formatting rules into a PostToolUse hook that runs prettier after every Edit or Write.
Move multi-step procedures into skills, and area-specific rules into .claude/rules files with a paths field.
Put personal settings in a gitignored CLAUDE.local.md, then check /context and run /doctor prompt-audit.
summary.stealThis: Before your next change to CLAUDE.md, run the one-line test on every line and move style rules into a formatter hook, migration recipes into a skill, and API rules into a path-scoped rule.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're watching Claude Code ignore rules in a CLAUDE.md that has grown past a couple hundred lines and want a concrete pruning checklist.
summary.quote: Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete CLAUDE.md pruning method (the one-line test) with a before-and-after file, a PostToolUse prettier hook, path-scoped .claude/rules, skills and CLAUDE.local.md, all accurately reflected in the card, though it largely repackages Anthropic's own docs and ends with a product upsell.

summary.title: AI Coding Agents: A Workflow That Holds Up
summary.idea: Agent output is cheap to produce but costly to understand, so write tickets with clear acceptance criteria, require a plan first, give the agent a check command, and cap diff size.
howItWorks: Write each task as a ticket: goal, constraints, done-when criteria, and an explicit out-of-scope list.
Ask the agent for a plan in read-only mode and check files touched, code reuse, and test approach.
Expose one check command (lint, typecheck, tests) and tell the agent to run it before finishing.
Fail CI when a diff exceeds a budget, for example 15 files or 400 changed lines.
Keep an AGENTS.md with commands, conventions and off-limits folders; add a line, ideally with a test, when a mistake repeats.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent task, add a CI diff-budget script that fails branches over about 15 files or 400 lines, so every agent change stays small enough to review properly.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing more agent-written pull requests than you can read carefully and want a simple ticket, plan, check and review loop.
summary.quote: A test the agent wrote for its own code can quietly confirm its own assumptions, so read those more closely than the code itself.

verdict.reason: Teaches concrete, copyable techniques (ticket template with out-of-scope list, plan-first review, single check command, and a working CI diff-budget script). The card matches the page accurately, but the material is fairly familiar best practice with no before/after evidence.

summary.title: timharris707/skills: 23 practical agent skills for non-engineers
summary.idea: Non-engineers who lead agents get misbuilt work and unreviewable diffs; this skill pack puts an orchestrator session in charge, with interview-first planning, multi-model decision review and proof-based PRs.
howItWorks: Each skill is a plain-markdown SKILL.md playbook the agent reads on its own, installed in one line and versioned.
The grilling skill interviews you in rounds until no load-bearing assumption remains; the agent fetches facts, you make decisions.
Advisory-board sends one decision to Claude, Codex, Gemini and Grok, who debate and return one recommendation plus a verdict.json for CI.
An orchestrate session routes work to parallel lanes and audits results, but never implements anything itself.
Handoff snapshots and show-me-your-work decision logs let a fresh session resume, and let you audit a table instead of a recap.
summary.stealThis: Before your next change big enough to argue about, have the agent run a grilling-style interview, asking you questions in rounds until nothing important is still assumed, before it writes any code.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're a non-engineer or lead who directs agents without reading code, and want ready-made skills for planning, review and handoff.
summary.quote: Every skill here started the same way: an agent failed me in a pattern, twice, and I got tired of re-explaining the fix.

verdict.reason: The author's actual skill pack grew out of repeated agent failures, and it has copyable techniques: a grilling interview before building, a multi-model advisory board that emits a CI-gateable verdict.json, handoff snapshots and append-only decision logs. The evidence is open SKILL.md files and example runs, but some skills are adapted from Matt Pocock's pack, and the setup fits people leading software builds better than other teams.

summary.title: How to review pull requests written by coding agents
summary.idea: Agent PRs look polished, which hides wrong-pattern fixes and missed dependents, so reviewers need a checklist aimed at agent failure modes and should move checks earlier to write time.
howItWorks: Read the diff first, then compare it with the agent's description; mismatches reveal unreported changes like altered defaults.
Find all callers of every changed function or type using grep or find-references, and treat 'no results' from tools as unknown.
Check the change against unwritten team rules, such as repository-layer database access or a single shared model client.
Scrutinise test diffs for loosened assertions, new skips and mocks, and inspect error paths for swallowed errors and silent fallbacks.
Shift checks earlier: record decisions with reasons in AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, require a caller list, and keep one concern per PR.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent task that changes a function signature, tell the agent to list every caller and update or explain each one in the PR description.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing several agent PRs a day and want a concrete checklist plus ideas for pushing checks earlier into the agent's task.
summary.quote: "No results" from a tool means "unknown", not "safe".

verdict.reason: The page teaches a tool-agnostic review checklist for agent PRs: read the diff before the description, grep every caller, and scrutinise test diffs and error paths, plus write-time fixes like making the agent list every caller of a changed signature; the vendor pitch at the end is separable, though evidence is thin beyond one caller-detection measurement.

summary.title: How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity
summary.idea: Agents that say 'done' without evidence ship mistakes, so these Java developers define task-specific verification gates, wrap deterministic checks around the model, and keep humans accountable for the result.
howItWorks: Ask the agent to interview you first, then review its plan for visible assumptions and defined verification gates.
Define done per task: the slide migration used screenshots, visual diffs, PDF comparison and content completeness checks.
Wrap Checkstyle, PMD and architecture checks into one report; hooks loop change, check, fix until no findings remain.
Update a reusable skill whenever a run teaches you something, so the next run starts with that lesson.
Point the agent at two likely files and require a unit test that fails on the old code.
summary.stealThis: Before your next refactor or migration, write a short list of evidence gates (tests passing, visual diff, no TODOs left) and require the agent to show proof for each before it can say done.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're tired of agents declaring victory without proof and want concrete examples of gates, quality-harness hooks and maintenance skills.
summary.quote: A good agent can execute the wrong idea incredibly quickly.

verdict.reason: Despite the vendor framing, the page teaches transferable techniques that work outside Copilot: task-specific evidence gates (screenshots, visual and PDF diffs for a migration), a hook-driven Checkstyle/PMD/architecture harness the agent loops on until clean, and requiring a unit test that fails on the old code; the examples are concrete, but there's no shared code or config.

summary.title: How Shopify turns open models into task experts
summary.idea: Token-heavy subagent work is slow and costly on frontier models, so Shopify defines a judged rubric, then repeatedly post-trains a small open model on self-healed production failures until it matches the frontier agent.
howItWorks: Product experts write a scoring rubric; an LLM judge is tuned until it agrees with held-out human labels.
An autoresearch loop tweaks prompts, tool descriptions or control flow one change at a time, keeping only changes that raise the judge score.
Each night the judge scores sampled production conversations; imperfect ones go to a self-healing step.
A frontier critic writes a hint, never the answer, and a simulated user reruns the request, up to three tries.
Passing reruns are anonymized and added to training data; humans fix the rest, which recalibrates the judge.
summary.stealThis: Before your next prompt or tool-description tweak on an agent, build a judge calibrated against human labels and keep a change only if the score improves.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agent subagents at scale and want a concrete loop for turning production failures into training data and cheaper models.
summary.quote: A frontier model acting as critic writes a hint, never the answer, and a simulated merchant reruns the request with it against the same store.

verdict.reason: The NVIDIA-heavy post-training parts are hard to copy, but the page does teach transferable techniques with real numbers: calibrate an LLM judge to human inter-rater agreement, keep agent tweaks only when the judge score rises, and self-heal failures with critic hints that never give the answer.

summary.title: Fragments: October 21
summary.idea: Agents debugging unfamiliar code go wrong when they read code first; Cindy Sridharan's approach has them gather raw evidence, pick a control, then test hypotheses against every fact.
howItWorks: Start the investigation by collecting raw facts about system behavior, not by reading source code.
Give the agent a control: a request, build or environment that does not show the bug.
Identify the signals that matter, discarding noisy data points that do not point to a hypothesis.
List hypotheses against signals in a table; signals that few hypotheses satisfy are the most valuable.
Validate each surviving hypothesis against every fact, treating each fact as a constraint on the solution.
summary.stealThis: The next time an agent chases a bug, tell it to collect logs and a working control case first, and to build a hypothesis-versus-facts table before it opens any code.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're debugging code you didn't write or no longer understand, and want a repeatable way to steer an agent's investigation.
summary.quote: having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern.

verdict.reason: Fowler's summary does teach Sridharan's debugging method: gather raw evidence and a control case before reading code, then validate hypotheses against every fact. It is a secondhand recap of a longer article with no code or transcripts, so it scores as thin, and the method is more about verification loops than harness design.

summary.title: Claude Mods: Flipping the Harness Inside Out
summary.idea: Agent output buries the things a human needs to notice, so Claude Mods let you write small code hooks that decide what the agent surfaces to you and when it interrupts.
howItWorks: A mod is a TypeScript or JavaScript plugin that hooks events like a prompt, tool call or interface render.
The built-in You Should Know mod runs a side agent that flags buried risks, such as uncommitted work in edited files.
Next Steps Supervisor fires only after turns that edit files, run commands or make 8+ tool calls, then offers a clickable next step.
Claude Code has a built-in plugin-authoring skill, so you describe the mod you want in plain language and Claude builds it.
Mods run unsandboxed with your permissions, so read any third-party mod's code first and keep an off switch like /supervisor off.
summary.stealThis: The next time you catch yourself manually re-checking the same thing after an agent turn, ask Claude to build a mod that checks it, and keep it only if it surfaces something you would have missed.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're customizing Claude Code and want concrete examples of mod hooks, plus honest notes on the noise, cost and trust tradeoffs.
summary.quote: did it surface something I would have missed, make a decision easier, or let me act without getting distracted by more output?

verdict.reason: It teaches a concrete harness technique: write Claude Code mods (event hooks such as a side-agent 'You Should Know' check and a turn-gated next-step supervisor) that decide what the agent surfaces to you, backed by a real example, usage numbers on noise and cost, and an open-source repo. The value is somewhat narrowed because it is tied to Claude Code.

summary.title: patch the planet
summary.idea: Temporary security workarounds turn into lasting tech debt because people forget to remove them; the fix is a dated reminder in AGENTS.MD so the agent later reassesses and backs the patch out itself.
howItWorks: Ask the agent whether your fleet is affected by the disclosed vulnerability; it checks the single declarative Nix source of truth.
The agent turns the finding into a plan, applies one fleet-wide patch, and it is committed and autodeployed.
Have the agent add a temporary reminder section to AGENTS.MD with a start date, such as five days out.
The reminder gives an exact check: is the upstream fix commit in the channel? If not, recheck two days later.
Once upstream has the fix, the agent bumps the pin, deletes the workaround files and imports, verifies the build, then deletes the reminder.
summary.stealThis: The next time you ship a temporary workaround, prompt your agent to add a dated AGENTS.MD section with the upstream check command, exact files to delete, a verification step, and an instruction to remove itself.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agents against infrastructure, especially Nix, and want to see the full reminder text and the patch-and-autodeploy flow.
summary.quote: You can prompt an agent to update the AGENTS.MD to automatically back out these patches

verdict.reason: The post teaches a concrete trick backed by the full reminder text: a dated, self-deleting AGENTS.MD section with an upstream check command, the exact files to delete, and a verification step, so the agent later backs out a temporary workaround itself. It is short and relies on the agent happening to run in that repo after the date, so it scores below the top tier.

summary.title: Agentic AI Reliability: Build a Testing Harness for Tool Use, Guardrails, Loops, & Workflow Outcomes
summary.idea: A fluent final answer can hide a broken workflow, so verify what the agent actually changed by checking authoritative state with a harness kept separate from the agent, rather than grading its wording.
howItWorks: Split the system into the agent under test, controlled test doubles, and a control plane holding expectations and evaluators.
Route every agent action through one gateway that validates arguments and enforces authorization and approval outside the agent.
Declare expected outcomes as state assertions, such as exactly one ticket and no credit, and check them against immutable snapshots.
Inject faults like timeouts at dependency boundaries and check the agent stops or fails faithfully instead of claiming success.
Record response, step, action, workflow and system verdicts separately, then gate releases on them.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent release, write a state-based assertion, such as one ticket created and no credit issued, and fail the run on that end state rather than on the agent's final message.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're moving a tool-using agent toward production and want a runnable reference harness with code for outcome verification, fault injection and release gates.
summary.quote: A good final answer doesn't prove that an agentic AI workflow was correct.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a concrete, transferable technique: declare expected outcomes as structured state assertions (count, field_match, absent) checked against immutable snapshots, kept apart from the agent, with gateway enforcement, fault injection and release gates. It backs this with a runnable open-source repo and code excerpts, and the card's claims match the page.

summary.title: personal-harness
summary.idea: Agent loops get expensive and drift when every role runs on whatever model the session holds; this repo pins a model and effort per role and keeps plan approval and commits with a human.
howItWorks: Flow is plan-dev, human plan approval, dev-loop, then commit-code; the loop stops at READY_TO_COMMIT and never commits itself.
plan-dev interviews you and locks an Acceptance Contract (per-task evidence) and Authority Boundaries (loop budget) before any code is written.
dev-loop modes: light runs two review axes, full runs four plus mutation testing, noreview runs none; the mode is frozen at start.
Every subagent pins its own model and effort in frontmatter; judgment roles get top tier, machine-checkable roles get medium effort.
Hooks enforce rg/fd, git identity and auto-format, and a Cursor guard refuses a spawn when the resolved model differs from the pin.
summary.stealThis: Before your next multi-step agent task, write an acceptance contract listing the evidence each TODO must produce, and have a human approve it before starting the loop.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running multi-agent loops across several tools and want a worked example of model tiering, review modes and guard hooks.
summary.quote: Dropping review drops the four reviewers, not the human's judgement.

verdict.reason: A real working harness repo that matches the card: per-role model and effort pins with a written rationale, an acceptance contract locked before the loop, human gates at triage and READY_TO_COMMIT, and a model-pin-guard hook; it's concrete and copyable but has no before/after evidence and is dense with platform-specific detail.

summary.title: Skills & Progressive Disclosure
summary.idea: Monolithic agent definitions load every checklist on every run, wasting context and diluting attention; keep the definition to identity and scope, and move procedures into skills loaded only when a task needs them.
howItWorks: Keep the always-loaded definition under about 50 lines: identity, scope, quality bar and a list of skill names.
Put step-by-step procedures, checklists, templates and tool-specific rules into separate skill files, such as SKILL.md under .claude/skills/.
Tell the agent to read only the skill matching the requested task, so a 2000-token definition becomes about 1000 tokens.
Make each skill self-contained, with no hidden 'load X first' dependency the agent might skip.
Keep the index synced with the filesystem, since a renamed or deleted skill leaves a broken reference and the agent guesses.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent run, cut your longest agent definition down to identity, scope and a list of skill names, and move each checklist into its own skill file.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running sub-agent fan-out or a bloated agent definition and want the token arithmetic and the failure modes of splitting it.
summary.quote: A monolithic agent definition embeds every checklist and procedure it might ever need, and pays for all of them on every run.

verdict.reason: It teaches a concrete, copyable pattern: cut the always-loaded agent definition to identity, scope and a skill index, and move procedures into self-contained SKILL.md files loaded per task. It includes an example index, token arithmetic and named failure modes (index rot, wrong skill, hidden dependencies), but the numbers are illustrative rather than a measured before and after.

summary.title: How to Keep AI-Generated Code Quality High Without Adding Reviewers
summary.idea: AI floods teams with large PRs, and adding reviewers doesn't fix the missing context. Put cheap control points before the human: small stacked PRs, acceptance criteria, codified review rules, and behavior checks.
howItWorks: Have the agent split work into a stack of small, dependent PRs instead of one large diff.
Write checkable acceptance criteria, including negative ones, and require a PR description explaining choices and what was not done.
Sort the last 100 review comments into rule-checkable, testable by running code, and genuine judgment; automate the first two.
Run the code in a preview environment, and scrutinize test diffs for removed assertions, skipped tests, and broadened mocks.
Spend human attention by blast radius: auth, payments, data and concurrency get depth; copy tweaks get a skim.
summary.stealThis: Before your next review round, pull the last 100 review comments and sort them into rule-checkable, testable, and judgment buckets, then write checks for the first bucket.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck reviewing agent-written PRs and want a layered, low-tooling way to cut the review load.
summary.quote: Green ≠ correct.

verdict.reason: Despite the vendor pitch at the end, the first half teaches product-independent techniques the card reports accurately: sorting the last 100 review comments into rule-checkable, testable and judgment buckets, negative acceptance criteria, and diffing tests for weakened assertions. It stays at 6 because evidence is thin, with no code or before-and-after.

summary.title: drj613/agent-skills: My personal agent skills/plugins
summary.idea: Skills scattered across tools and machines are hard to reuse, so this repo bundles curated skills, agents and extensions and keeps harness-specific details in one config file so they run anywhere.
howItWorks: Run /setup-harness once per repo to write .agent-harness.md, which holds model IDs, tracker choice and transcript paths.
Skills read that file when present and fall back to generic behavior like 'strongest models available' when it is missing.
pi-install.sh copies skills and agents into Pi's global dirs and rewrites Claude Code tool names to Pi's built-ins.
Verification skills generate a project-local skill that drives the real app and captures evidence, then keep it current as the app changes.
team-review runs parallel domain specialists, validates findings with code, dedupes via a judge, then loops through fix, defer or dismiss.
summary.stealThis: Move model names, tracker and path settings out of your skills into one repo-root .agent-harness.md, so the next time you switch tools or machines the skills work unchanged.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're maintaining a personal skill library across several agent tools and want a working example of portable skills, verification skills and review loops.
summary.quote: model IDs, tracker paths, and tooling live in .agent-harness.md, so the skills run in Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Pi, and friends.

verdict.reason: Mostly a round-up of other people's skills, but the README does teach one concrete, copyable pattern: move model IDs, tracker and paths into a repo-root .agent-harness.md that skills read, with a generic fallback, and translate tool names on install. The explanation is thin and there is little evidence, so it only scrapes a pass.
